title: Ezekiel 30:1–19
context: Ezekiel 30:1–19 is an undated oracle in which the LORD tells the prophet to wail over the coming day of the LORD on Egypt. The day is near, a day of clouds and a time of the nations. A sword will come on Egypt and its allies, including Ethiopia, Put, Lud, and others, some of whose locations are uncertain, and those who support Egypt will fall. The LORD names Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon as the one by whose hand Egypt’s multitude will end. He will dry the rivers, destroy the idols of Memphis, and bring judgment on a long list of Egyptian cities, from Pathros and Zoan to No, Sin, Aven, Pibeseth, and Tehaphnehes. Many identify No with Thebes and Tehaphnehes with the Tahpanhes of Jeremiah 43:7–9, though some identifications remain debated. The refrain that they will know that the LORD is God runs through the unit. Both traditions read it as showing that the day of the LORD, often announced against Israel, also reaches the nations (compare Joel 2:1 and Zephaniah 1:14).

verses.text: The LORD’s word came again to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet reports that the LORD’s word came to him again. Arminians see the continuation of God’s message against Egypt, which the prophet faithfully delivers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as introducing an undated oracle. Both traditions note that this unit has no date of its own, unlike the oracles around it, and they read it within the Egypt collection.

verses.text: “Son of man, prophesy, and say, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Wail, ‘Alas for the day!’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet to wail, "Alas for the day!" Arminian readers see a call to lament, showing that the coming judgment is a matter of grief and not of glee.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the cry as announcing the seriousness of the coming day. Both traditions read the wailing as fitting for a day of judgment, whether on Israel or on the nations.

verses.text: For the day is near, even the LORD’s day is near. It will be a day of clouds, a time of the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the day is near, the day of the LORD, a day of clouds and a time for the nations. Arminians see the day of the LORD as a time of judgment that reaches beyond Israel to all nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign rule over history. Both traditions compare Joel 2:1 and Zephaniah 1:14, where the day of the LORD is also said to be near, and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: A sword will come on Egypt, and anguish will be in Ethiopia, when the slain fall in Egypt. They take away her multitude, and her foundations are broken down.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says a sword will come on Egypt and anguish on Ethiopia as the slain fall and Egypt’s foundations are broken. Arminian readers see the judgment spreading to Egypt’s allies, who shared in its pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the judgment shaking Egypt’s very foundations. Both traditions read Ethiopia here as the land to Egypt’s south, often called Cush, which was closely tied to Egypt at times.

verses.text: “ ‘ “Ethiopia, Put, Lud, all the mixed people, Cub, and the children of the land that is allied with them, will fall with them by the sword.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Ethiopia, Put, Lud, mixed peoples, Cub, and Egypt’s allies will fall by the sword. Arminians see the reach of God’s judgment over all who joined Egypt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over many peoples. Both traditions note that some of these names, especially Cub, are uncertain, and they avoid confident identifications.

verses.text: “ ‘The LORD says: “They also who uphold Egypt will fall. The pride of her power will come down. They will fall by the sword in it from the tower of Seveneh,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says those who uphold Egypt will fall and the pride of its power will come down. Arminian readers see judgment falling on pride, which leads nations to trust in their own strength.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God bringing down human power. Both traditions read the verse as continuing the theme of 29:10, using the same phrase about the tower of Seveneh to mark the whole land.

verses.text: “They will be desolate in the middle of the countries that are desolate. Her cities will be among the cities that are wasted.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Egypt will be desolate among desolate countries and its cities among ruined cities. Arminians see Egypt sharing the fate of the nations it once dominated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as echoing 29:12. Both traditions see the repetition as reinforcing the certainty of the judgment.

verses.text: They will know that I am the LORD when I have set a fire in Egypt, and all her helpers are destroyed.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they will know he is the LORD when he sets fire to Egypt and destroys its helpers. Arminian readers see judgment as revealing God, so that even those who suffer it come to recognize who he is.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s purpose to display his glory. Both traditions hold the recognition formula as shared ground, a repeated theme throughout Ezekiel.

verses.text: “ ‘ “In that day messengers will go out from before me in ships to make the careless Ethiopians afraid. There will be anguish on them, as in the day of Egypt; for, behold, it comes.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says messengers will go out in ships to terrify the careless Ethiopians, and anguish will come on them. Arminians see news of Egypt’s fall spreading to its neighbors, who had felt secure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reach of God’s judgment. Both traditions read the ships as moving up the Nile, and they note that the careless Ethiopians are pictured as overconfident.

verses.text: “ ‘The Lord GOD says: “I will also make the multitude of Egypt to cease, by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says he will end Egypt’s multitude by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. Arminian readers see God naming the instrument of judgment, which shows his control over the course of events.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over the nations. Both traditions note that how God uses Babylon is discussed at the Judges 9:23 box.

verses.text: He and his people with him, the terrible of the nations, will be brought in to destroy the land. They will draw their swords against Egypt, and fill the land with the slain.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar and his people, the most terrible of nations, will come to destroy the land and fill it with the slain. Arminians see the severity of the coming invasion, which God permits and directs as judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s hand in the invasion. Both traditions read the phrase terrible of the nations as describing Babylon’s reputation for ruthlessness, which appears elsewhere in Ezekiel (28:7).

verses.text: I will make the rivers dry, and will sell the land into the hand of evil men. I will make the land desolate, and all that is therein, by the hand of foreigners. I, the LORD, have spoken it.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will dry the rivers, sell the land to evil men, and make it desolate by foreigners’ hands. Arminian readers see the loss of the Nile’s blessing, which was the source of Egypt’s life and pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s power over nature and nations. Both traditions note the closing words, I, the LORD, have spoken it, as underlining the certainty of the judgment.

verses.text: “ ‘The Lord GOD says: “I will also destroy the idols, and I will cause the images to cease from Memphis. There will be no more a prince from the land of Egypt. I will put a fear in the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says he will destroy the idols of Memphis, end Egypt’s princes, and put fear in the land. Arminians see God’s judgment on false worship, showing that Egypt’s gods cannot protect it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the LORD’s supremacy over the gods of Egypt. Both traditions compare the judgment on Egypt’s gods in Exodus 12:12, and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: I will make Pathros desolate, and will set a fire in Zoan, and will execute judgments on No.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will make Pathros desolate, set fire to Zoan, and execute judgments on No. Arminian readers see judgment reaching Egypt’s major cities, from south to north.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the thoroughness of the judgment. Both traditions note that No is usually identified with Thebes and Zoan with Tanis in the Delta, though they hold these identifications with some care.

verses.text: I will pour my wrath on Sin, the stronghold of Egypt. I will cut off the multitude of No.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will pour wrath on Sin, Egypt’s stronghold, and cut off the multitude of No. Arminians see God’s judgment reaching even Egypt’s fortified places, which offered no security.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the futility of strongholds against God. Both traditions note that Sin is often identified with Pelusium, a fortress city in the eastern Delta, though this is not certain.

verses.text: I will set a fire in Egypt Sin will be in great anguish. No will be broken up. Memphis will have adversaries in the daytime.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will set fire to Egypt, Sin will be in anguish, No will be broken, and Memphis will face enemies by day. Arminian readers see the repetition of cities as stressing that no part of Egypt will escape.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the poetic list as underlining the completeness of the judgment. Both traditions read the verse as part of a sweeping survey of Egypt’s cities.

verses.text: The young men of Aven and of Pibeseth will fall by the sword. They will go into captivity.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the young men of Aven and Pibeseth will fall by the sword and go into captivity. Arminians see the human cost of the judgment, as the young are killed or taken away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing the effects of war on Egypt’s cities. Both traditions note that Aven is often identified with On or Heliopolis and Pibeseth with Bubastis, though these remain identifications rather than certainties.

verses.text: At Tehaphnehes also the day will withdraw itself, when I break the yokes of Egypt there. The pride of her power will cease in her. As for her, a cloud will cover her, and her daughters will go into captivity.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the day will grow dark at Tehaphnehes when he breaks Egypt’s yokes, its pride will end, and its daughters go into captivity. Arminian readers see the end of Egypt’s oppressive power, which God himself brings about.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God breaking Egypt’s power. Both traditions note that Tehaphnehes is likely the Tahpanhes where Judean refugees went (Jeremiah 43:7–9), and they read the cloud as a picture of judgment.

verses.text: Thus I will execute judgments on Egypt. Then they will know that I am the LORD.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will execute judgments on Egypt, and they will know he is the LORD. Arminians see the unit’s conclusion, where judgment leads to recognition of God’s identity and power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s glory as the goal of his judgments. Both traditions hold the recognition formula as shared ground, which closes the oracle as it does many others in Ezekiel.
